questions.knowledge_point: Finding Two Scalar Factors in a Linear Combination
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14044176/assets/01940c9fa894d635300a49867da35d483b873a45d2a75204c20c58e4cb84c883.png)

Consider the picture above. Given that $t=\lambda r+\mu s$, find $\lambda $ and $\mu .$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14044176/assets/a0d9fa1c366945e5e789b6361f929357af163db2e9be4a3ccc9023c12486aca6.png)

In $△ORT$ shown above, we have:

- $OR=2|r|$

- $\overset{\to }{OR}$ has the opposite direction to $r$

Hence, $\overset{\to }{OR}=-2r.$

Similarly:

- $RT=2|s|$

- $\overset{\to }{RT}$ has the opposite direction to $s$

Hence, $\overset{\to }{RT}=-2s.$

Additionally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}t & =\overset{\to }{OR}+\overset{\to }{RT} \\  & =-2r-2s.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $t=\lambda r+\mu s=-2r-2s.$ 

Since $s∦r,$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients, we get:

- $\lambda =-2$ and $\mu =-2$

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing a Vector That Satisfies a Ratio in Terms of Known Vectors
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14044176/assets/50b87e86bd2985e54ce0a8fe6b3e23986f7e1946a5284d0ae297d96b9cbc60f6.png)

Consider the diagram above, where $\overset{\to }{OM}=m,$ $\overset{\to }{ON}=n$ and $P$ divides $\overset{―}{MN}$ in the ratio $MP:PN=2:1.$ Find $\overset{\to }{OP}.$
questions.worked_solution:
From the diagram, we see that

$$
\overset{\to }{OP}=\overset{\to }{OM}+\overset{\to }{MP}.
$$

We're told that $\overset{\to }{OM}=m,$ so we just need to work out $\overset{\to }{MP}.$

First, from $△OMN,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{MN} & =\overset{\to }{MO}+\overset{\to }{ON} \\  & =-\overset{\to }{OM}+\overset{\to }{ON} \\  & =-m+n \\  & =n-m.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $MP:PN=2:1,$ we have

$$
\overset{\to }{MP}=\frac{2}{3}\overset{\to }{MN}=\frac{2}{3}(n-m).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OP} & =\overset{\to }{OM}+\overset{\to }{MP} \\  & =m+\frac{2}{3}(n-m) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}m+\frac{2}{3}n.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the diagram above, where $\overset{\to }{OA}=a,$ $\overset{\to }{OQ}=q,$ and $N$ divides $\overset{―}{AQ}$ in the ratio $AN:NQ=12:7.$ Express $\overset{\to }{ON}$ via the vectors $a$ and $q.$

$\,\overset{\to }{ON}=$
{{field-1}}
$a+$
{{field-2}}
$q$
questions.worked_solution:
From the diagram, we see that

$$
\overset{\to }{ON}=\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{AN}.
$$

We're told that $\overset{\to }{OA}=a,$ so we just need to work out $\overset{\to }{AN}.$

First, from $△OAQ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AQ} & =\overset{\to }{AO}+\overset{\to }{OQ} \\  & =-\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{OQ} \\  & =-a+q \\  & =q-a.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $AN:NQ=12:7,$ we have

$$
\overset{\to }{AN}=\frac{12}{19}\overset{\to }{AQ}=\frac{12}{19}(q-a).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{ON} & =\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{AN} \\  & =a+\frac{12}{19}(q-a) \\  & =\frac{7}{19}a+\frac{12}{19}q.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:

Consider the picture above. If $c=\lambda a-2b,$ then$\,\lambda =$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find $\lambda ,$ we want to match the expression

$$
c=\lambda a-2b.
$$

We are given that one of the components is $-2b.$ So, we first draw the vector $-2b$ from the origin. Then we complete the path to the point $C.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14044176/assets/7e6923e8b8b774eeaa2f885ec6aa24bb03f07c547fa50e7145a4113a18e92e8a.png)

Let $P$ be the endpoint of the vector $-2b.$ Then

$$
c=\overset{\to }{OP}+\overset{\to }{PC}.
$$

In $△OPC,$ we have:

- $PC=2|a|$

- $\overset{\to }{PC}$ and $a$ have opposite directions

Hence, $\overset{\to }{PC}=-2a.$

Additionally,

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =\overset{\to }{OP}+\overset{\to }{PC} \\  & =-2b-2a.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $c=\lambda a-2b=-2a-2b.$

Since $a∦b,$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients of $a,$ we get:

$$
\lambda =-2
$$
